gloss: cover (the sinner and sin, a life, the holy things); ransom; coat with pitch
summary: כפר is literally to cover. The qal coats the ark with pitch, inside and out (Gen 6:14); the piel כִּפֶּר covers the sinner, the flesh made unclean as well as the sins done, and the land and the holy things, mostly with the blood of an offering, for “the blood covers by the life” (Lev 17:11), and the כֹּפֶר is the covering price given for a life that is forfeit (Exo 30:12–16; Num 35:31–33). Scripture sets beside the covering what it achieves: sin blotted out and departed, the altar purified, wrath turned back (Jer 18:23; Isa 6:7; Ezk 43:26; Num 25:11). Its nouns name יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים, the day of coverings on the tenth of the seventh month (Lev 23:27–28), and the כַּפֹּרֶת, the gold covering of the ark on which that day’s blood was sprinkled; Arabic kafara is “cover”, and Akkadian kapāru both “smear on” and “wipe clean”. A young lion, villages, henna, frost and bowls share the spelling; their links to covering are not clear.

words.gloss: cover (a person and their sin); ransom, appease; coat with pitch
words.summary: Almost all its uses are piel. What it covers is first the person or land (with עַל or בְּעַד): the flesh in its unclean state, such as a mother after childbirth or a healed leper who has done no wrong, as well as the sin and iniquity done; then the altar and holy place made unclean by dwelling among Israel’s uncleanness, and an angry face. What covers is blood, an offering, a payment, or another’s life; and what follows is cleanness, sin taken away, forgiveness and wrath turned. The single qal coats the ark with pitch (כֹּפֶר).

senses.definition: Coat a surface with pitch, inside and out; said with its own noun כֹּפֶר.

evidence.note: “Coat it (וְכָפַרְתָּ) inside and outside with pitch (בַּכֹּפֶר).”

stems.gloss: cover (a person and their sin, the holy things); ransom, appease

senses.definition: Cover sin or iniquity so that it no longer stands before God, and cover the altar and holy place, which did not sin, against the defilement they take on from dwelling among Israel’s uncleanness. Scripture sets beside it what the covering does: “blot out”, “depart”, “purify” and “cleanse”.

evidence.note: “Do not cover (תְּכַפֵּר) their iniquity, and do not blot out (תֶּמְחִי) their sin from before you.”
Seven days they shall purge (יְכַפְּרוּ) the altar and cleanse (וְטִהֲרוּ) it.
Blood on the altar’s horns: “you shall purify it (וְחִטֵּאתָ) and purge it (וְכִפַּרְתָּהוּ).”
He makes a covering for the holy place because of the uncleannesses of Israel and their transgressions, and so for the tent, which dwells with them in the midst of their uncleanness.
Being compassionate, he covered iniquity and did not destroy them; he turned back his anger.
“Our transgressions, you cover them.”
“Deliver us and cover our sins for your name’s sake.”
Beside “to finish transgression” and “to end sins”: “to cover iniquity”.
When Yahweh covers for Jerusalem all that she has done.

senses.definition: Cover a person, people or land, with עַל or בְּעַד, mostly by the blood of an offering. What is covered is the person in their state as well as their deeds: a covering is made for a mother after childbirth and for a healed leper, who have done no wrong, as for one who has sinned; and the outcome is that they are clean or forgiven.

evidence.note: “The priest shall make a covering for them, and they will be forgiven.”
“On this day he will make a covering for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you will be clean before Yahweh.”
No work on יוֹם כִּפֻּרִים, “to make a covering for you before Yahweh your God.”
The life of the flesh is in the blood, given on the altar to make a covering for your lives; the blood covers by the life.
After childbirth: “the priest shall make a covering for her, and she will be clean.” She has done no wrong; it is her flesh that is covered.
The burnt offering is accepted for him, to make a covering for him.
The priest makes a covering for the healed man, and he is clean.
Aaron makes a covering for the Levites to cleanse them.
He will make a covering for his land, his people.

senses.gloss: avert wrath by a ransom or gift; appease
senses.definition: Turn away the anger or death due by covering it with something given in place of the life forfeited: a payment, a gift, or another’s life.

evidence.note: The half shekel, the כֹּפֶר of each man’s life (Exo 30:12), is given “to make a covering for your lives.”
Jacob: “I will appease (אֲכַפְּרָה) his face with the gift that goes before me.”
A king’s wrath is messengers of death, but a wise man will appease it.
David asks the Gibeonites “with what shall I make a covering?”; they want no silver or gold, but lives (2Sa 21:4–6).
Wrath has gone out and the plague begun; Aaron makes a covering with incense and the plague stops (Num 17:12–13).
Phinehas made a covering for Israel; he turned back Yahweh’s wrath (Num 25:11).
The officers bring gold “to make a covering for our lives before Yahweh” after the count.
Moses goes up to Yahweh: “perhaps I can make a covering for your sin.”
A ruin will fall on Babylon that she cannot ward off (כַּפְּרָהּ).

senses.definition: Of iniquity, be covered and so taken away; of a covenant, be made void; of a land, have its bloodguilt covered.

evidence.note: “Your iniquity has departed (וְסָר), and your sin is covered (תְּכֻפָּר).”
Jacob’s iniquity covered, parallel to “the removing of his sin.”
“Your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand.”
No covering can be made for the land for blood shed in it except by the blood of the one who shed it.
“This iniquity will not be covered for you until you die.”
By covenant faithfulness and truth iniquity is covered.
The priests eat what the covering was made with.

senses.definition: Of iniquity, be covered by sacrifice or offering.

evidence.note: The iniquity of Eli’s house will never be covered by sacrifice or offering.

senses.definition: Of shed blood, have its guilt covered from the people.

evidence.note: “Cover for your people Israel … and the blood will be covered them.”

parallels.note: Wiping away iniquity set beside blotting out sin.
Sin covered beside iniquity departing, and its removal.
Purging the altar beside cleansing it, and a covering made to cleanse.

words.gloss: coverings (of the people and their sins)
words.summary: Always plural, “coverings”. It names the yearly day of the seventh month, on which a covering was made for the people, the priests and the holy things as well as their sins, the sin offering and ram by which a covering was made for a man, and once the silver given as the people’s ransom.

senses.definition: The covering made for the people and their sins, above all on יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים, the tenth day of the seventh month, and in the offerings made for it.

evidence.note: “On the tenth of this seventh month is יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים.”
“It is יוֹם כִּפֻּרִים, to make a covering for you before Yahweh your God.”
Once a year Aaron puts the blood of the sin offering of the כִּפֻּרִים on the horns of the incense altar.
The horn sounds on יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים to begin the jubilee.
A bull of sin offering each day for the כִּפֻּרִים, when the altar was consecrated.
The ram of the כִּפֻּרִים, by which a covering is made for the man.
The sin offering of the כִּפֻּרִים on the tenth of the seventh month.

senses.definition: The silver paid as ransom for the lives of those counted.

evidence.note: “The silver of the כִּפֻּרִים” from the census, “to make a covering for your lives.”

evidence.locator: Lev.25.9, הַכִּפֻּרִים → ἱλασμοῦ; Num.5.8, הַכִּפֻּרִים → ἱλασμοῦ

phrases.gloss: יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים, the Day of Coverings, the tenth of the seventh month

words.summary: The gold covering laid on the ark, from which Yahweh spoke and on which the blood of יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים was sprinkled: a noun of the piel, “the covering”, set over the testimony inside the ark.

senses.gloss: the covering of the ark, the place of covering
senses.definition: A slab of pure gold the size of the ark, with the two cherubim of one piece with it, set on the ark above the testimony; Yahweh meets and speaks from above it, and once a year the high priest sprinkles blood on it and before it.

evidence.note: Pure gold, two and a half cubits by one and a half: the ark’s own length and width.
“Put the כַּפֹּרֶת on the ark, above; and in the ark put the testimony.”
“I will meet with you there, and speak with you from above the כַּפֹּרֶת, from between the two cherubim.”
The high priest sprinkles the bull’s blood on the כַּפֹּרֶת and seven times before it.
Yahweh appears in the cloud over the כַּפֹּרֶת.
The people’s goat: its blood too on the כַּפֹּרֶת and before it.
Moses hears the voice speaking from above the כַּפֹּרֶת.
The inner room is “the house of the כַּפֹּרֶת.”

evidence.locator: Exo.25.17, כַּפֹּרֶת → ἱλαστήριον; Lev.16.14, הַכַּפֹּרֶת → ἱλαστηρίου

words.gloss: ransom, the price of a life

senses.definition: What is given in place of a forfeited life, to free the one whose life is due.

evidence.note: If a כֹּפֶר is laid on the owner of the goring ox, he gives “the redemption price of his life” (פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ).
Each man gives “the כֹּפֶר of his life” to Yahweh when counted, so that no plague strikes them.
“You shall take no כֹּפֶר for the life of a murderer … he shall surely die.”
No man can redeem (פָּדֹה) his brother or give God his כֹּפֶר.
“I give Egypt as your כֹּפֶר, Cush and Seba in your place.”
No כֹּפֶר for the manslayer to leave his city of refuge early.
“Deliver him from going down to the pit; I have found a כֹּפֶר.”
The ransom of a man’s life is his riches.
The wicked is a ransom for the righteous.
The wronged husband will accept no כֹּפֶר.
A great ransom will not turn you aside.

senses.definition: A payment that buys off justice.

evidence.note: “From whose hand have I taken a כֹּפֶר to blind my eyes with it?”
Takers of a כֹּפֶר, who turn aside the needy in the gate.

parallels.note: The ransom laid on a man is the redemption price of his life.
Giving God a ransom set beside redeeming a brother.

words.summary: Once, with its verb, for the coat of the ark. Akkadian, Aramaic and Arabic all have this noun for pitch or bitumen.

senses.definition: The waterproof coating put on the ark inside and out.

evidence.note: “Coat it inside and outside with pitch (בַּכֹּפֶר).”

words.summary: A lion grown enough to hunt for itself. Scripture’s young lion lies under cover: it sits “in hidden places” (Psa 17:12), crouches in its dens and waits in the covert (Job 38:39–40), and leaves its covert when its land is laid waste (Jer 25:38). So it may be named as the one that lies covered, as Arabic كَافِر is a man who stays in a place and hides himself. Its roar lays waste a land and its cities (Jer 2:15), but scripture does not speak of it covering the land. The link is not certain.

senses.definition: A lion past the cub stage that has learned to hunt and roars for prey; an image of strength, boldness and danger.

evidence.note: The lioness rears one of her cubs; he becomes a כְּפִיר, learns to tear prey, and devours men.
“A כְּפִיר of lions came roaring to meet him.”
Parallel to the אַרְיֵה roaring over prey.
The young lions roar for prey and seek their food from God.
Young lions lack and go hungry, but those who seek Yahweh lack no good thing.
The righteous are bold as a כְּפִיר.
Yahweh is like a lion to Ephraim and like a כְּפִיר to Judah.
Calf and young lion together, led by a little child.
Like a lion eager to tear, “like a כְּפִיר sitting in hidden places.”
The young lions crouch in their dens and sit in the covert to lie in wait.
“He has left his covert like the כְּפִיר.”
Young lions roar over him and make his land a waste, his cities burned.

parallels.note: The lion, set beside the young lion.

words.summary: An open settlement in the countryside, as against a city. Akkadian, Phoenician, Ugaritic and Syriac have the word; Arabic took it from Syriac. Scripture’s villages stand among the fields (Sng 7:12; 1Ch 27:25). Arabic calls the sower كَافِر because he covers the seed with earth, and calls the earth كَفْر because it covers what is beneath it, so the village may be the place of those who cover the seed; scripture does not show the link, and it is not certain.

senses.definition: A small unwalled settlement among the fields.

evidence.note: “Let us go out to the field; let us lodge in the villages.”
Storehouses in the field, in the cities, in the villages and in the towers.

words.summary: Once, in construct, as another form of כָּפָר.

senses.definition: An open country settlement, as against a fortified city.

evidence.note: “From the fortified city to the village of the open country (כֹּפֶר הַפְּרָזִי).”

words.summary: Once, with the article, where Sanballat asks Nehemiah to meet him. It may be “the villages” in the plain of Ono, or a place called Kephirim; the text does not settle which.

senses.definition: A meeting place in the plain of Ono; either open villages or a town of that name.

evidence.note: “Come, let us meet together בַּכְּפִירִים in the plain of Ono.”

words.summary: A fragrant flowering shrub of the garden and vineyard, spoken of as a cluster (אֶשְׁכֹּל) of blossom. Aramaic has the same word. Arabic كَافُور is the sheath that covers a palm’s blossom and the calyx that covers a vine’s unopened cluster, “because it covers what is within it”, and henna is itself a paste smeared on as a dye, as the qal smears pitch; either may give the name. Scripture does not show the link, and it is not certain.

senses.definition: A shrub whose clusters of blossoms are prized for their scent, named among spices.

evidence.note: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna in the vineyards of En Gedi.”
Henna with nard among the fruits of the garden.

words.summary: The thin white frost lying on the ground. Scripture sets it on the earth, on the face of the wilderness (Exo 16:14), and scattered like ashes (Psa 147:16): a thin covering over the ground. Aramaic has the same word. The link to covering is drawn from how the frost lies, not stated, and is not certain.

senses.definition: Frost lying fine and white on the ground, set beside snow and ice as things God makes.

evidence.note: The manna lay fine “as the frost on the ground.”
He gives snow like wool and scatters frost like ashes.
Parallel to ice: “the frost of heaven, who gave birth to it?”

words.summary: A gold or silver bowl among the temple vessels, in the later books only. Aramaic has the same word. Scripture only counts and weighs the bowls and never describes their use or shape, so nothing shows whether they were covered, or spread wide; the link to the root’s sense is not clear.

senses.definition: A vessel of gold or silver for the temple, counted and weighed.

evidence.note: David gives the gold and silver by weight for each כְּפוֹר.
Thirty gold bowls and 410 silver bowls returned from Babylon.
Twenty gold bowls worth a thousand darics.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s verb for denying: Peter denying Jesus, denying oneself, refusing. Aramaic uses כְּפַר so, and Arabic كُفْر is denial and ingratitude, which the Arabic lexicographers explain as covering over: one covers a benefit received, or what is so, that it may not be seen. Peter covers over that he knows Jesus to shield himself (Mat 26:69–74), and Arabic also uses the root of a man covering himself with arms or a garment (تَكَفَّرَ); to deny oneself is then to cover over one’s own self. That link to the Hebrew is through the cognates, not shown by scripture.

senses.definition: Say one does not know or belong to someone, or that something is not so; refuse to own.

evidence.note: “Whoever denies me before people, I also will deny him before my Father.”
Peter denied before them all: “I do not know what you are saying.”
John confessed and did not deny.
“Let him deny himself and take up his cross.”
All denied having touched him.
The liar is the one who denies that Jesus is the Messiah.
They confess God, but deny him by their works.
He has denied the faith.

senses.definition: Refuse an offered name or a person sent.

evidence.note: Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.
The Moses whom they rejected, God sent as ruler and deliverer.

senses.definition: Be disowned.

evidence.note: Whoever denies me before people will be denied before the angels of God.

senses.definition: One who does not acknowledge kindness received.

evidence.note: The Most High is kind to the evil and to the ungrateful.

senses.definition: One who disowns the kindness shown him.

evidence.note: In the last days people will be “deniers of grace” (ἀχάριστοι).

words.summary: Once, for the Greek περίψημα, “what is wiped off”. It keeps the sense of wiping that Akkadian and Aramaic kpr have.

senses.definition: What is wiped off and thrown away; of the apostles as the world treats them.

evidence.note: “We have become as the filth of the world, the refuse of everyone, until now.”

senses.definition: A small country settlement, named beside villages.

evidence.note: The crowds sent to the villages and hamlets around to find lodging and food.

cognates.gloss: wipe (clean), wipe clean cultically, rub; coat, smear
cognates.note: One verb for both motions the Hebrew root shows: wiping a thing clean, including in rites, and smearing a coat on. Oracc’s senses for it include “(cultically) wipe clean”, “rub”, “coat” and “smear”.

evidence.locator: armep x000031150, kapāru [wipe (clean)] V; armep x000099830, kapāru [wipe clean] (kuppuru); armep x000039370, kapāru [smear] V

cognates.note: A noun of kapāru for the result of cultic wiping, as כִּפֻּרִים is the noun of the piel. Rare (five attestations, Neo-Assyrian).
In a Neo-Punic votive prayer (Teboursouk): “support them, help them up, forgive them (kprm)!”
Known from the place name kprʾ, the Phoenician name of Solus in Sicily.
From Anderson and Moser’s root set only; not yet checked in a Ugaritic dictionary.

cognates.gloss: wipe out, efface; forgive, cover; (ithpe.) be wiped out, be forgiven
cognates.note: Jastrow’s first example of the plain sense is the Targum of Pro 30:20, where the Hebrew has מָחֲתָה, “she wipes her mouth”.
The Targum Onkelos uses it at Gen 6:14.

evidence.locator: K00997, כְּפוֹרָא I, Targ. Y. II Exo 16:14

cognates.gloss: veil, hide, cover; cover sown seed with earth
cognates.note: Lane derives from this “covering” the sower (كَافِر, he covers the seed), the night and dark cloud, and the palm spathe (كَافُور, it covers what is within).

cognates.gloss: cover, efface, annul (a sin); expiate; (كَفَّارَة) expiation, as for a broken oath or for unintended homicide
cognates.note: Lane: كَفَّرَ ٱللّٰهُ عَنْهُ الذَّنْبَ “God effaced his sin”; the كَفَّارَة is what effaces a sin or crime, among them the payment for unintentional homicide, where the Hebrew has כֹּפֶר.

cognates.gloss: tar, pitch, with which ships are smeared

evidence.locator: p. 2621, root كفر, كُفْرٌ (n37102), second sense

cognates.gloss: ingratitude, denial of a benefit; disbelief; (كَافَرَ) deny someone his right
cognates.note: Lane’s sources take كَفَرَ النِّعْمَةَ, “he was ungrateful for the favour”, as a use of كَفَرَ “cover”: one covers over a benefit received.
Lane’s sources call it a Syriac word, used mostly in Syria and Egypt: a loan from Aramaic into Arabic, not an independent witness.

cognates.gloss: one who stays in a place and hides himself; one covered with arms; (تَكَفَّرَ) cover oneself with arms or a garment
cognates.note: Uses of كَفَرَ “cover” for a man under cover: lying hidden in a place, or wrapped in armour or a garment.

evidence.locator: p. 2621, root كفر, تكفّر بِالسِّلَاحِ (n37100); p. 2622, كَافِرٌ (n37110)

doctrine.statement: The first covering in scripture is of nakedness. When the eyes of the man and the woman were opened they knew they were naked, and they sewed fig leaves and made themselves girdles (Gen 3:7); they hid from Yahweh, and the man said, “I was afraid, because I was naked” (Gen 3:10–11). Yahweh God then made for them כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר, coats of a skin, and clothed them (Gen 3:21): the coats are plural, the skin is singular, so one animal’s life was given and its one skin covered both of them. What was covered was the flesh their sin had changed, now under death (Gen 3:19), not the deed itself. Gen 3 does not use כפר or name the animal, but the pattern of scripture supplies it. Peter speaks of three heavens and earths: the world of old, made by the word of God, the heavens and earth which are now, and the new heavens and new earth to come (2Pe 3:5–7, 13). The Mosaic world was founded at the Passover with a lamb, one for each house, whose blood on the door kept the household from death (Exo 12:3–7, 13); the world to come rests on Christ our Passover, sacrificed for us (1Co 5:7), “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (Jhn 1:29), by whose precious blood we are redeemed, “as of a lamb without blemish and without spot”, foreknown before the foundation of the world (1Pe 1:19–20). Revelation names him the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world (Rev 13:8). With a lamb at the founding of the second world and of the third, the one skin in the garden at the founding of the first completes the pattern: a lamb slain in the garden. The Law keeps the same line: the priest makes a covering for a mother after childbirth, with a lamb or two birds, and she is clean (Lev 12:6–8), though she has done no wrong, and Mary brought that offering (Luk 2:22–24); on יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים he makes a covering for the holy place and the tent, which did not sin, because they dwell among Israel’s uncleanness (Lev 16:16), and Aaron first makes a covering for himself and his house (Lev 16:6, 11). So Christ: God made him sin for us who knew no sin (2Co 5:21), sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and, for sin, condemned sin in the flesh (Rom 8:3); he did no sin (1Pe 2:22) yet shared flesh and blood, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death (Heb 2:14), being made like his brothers in all things to make a covering for the sins of the people (ἱλάσκεσθαι, Heb 2:17), and he offered up himself once (Heb 7:27; 9:12): as one skin covered the man and the woman, by one offering he has perfected for all time those who are made holy (Heb 10:14). Those baptised into him have put him on (Gal 3:27), and he counsels white garments, that the shame of nakedness may not appear (Rev 3:18), until the mortal is swallowed up by life (2Co 5:2–4).

Scripture ties the verb to כֹּפֶר, a price given for a life that is forfeit. When Israel was counted, each man gave a half shekel as “the כֹּפֶר of his life” so that no plague would strike them; rich and poor gave the same, “to make a covering for your lives” (Exo 30:12–16). For a murderer no כֹּפֶר may be taken, and blood shed on the land can be covered only by the blood of the one who shed it (Num 35:31–33). Yahweh gives blood on the altar for this: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and the blood covers by the life (Lev 17:11). No man can give God the ransom for his brother, for the redemption of a life is costly (Psa 49:8–9); in Job a messenger pleading for a man says, “Deliver him from going down to the pit; I have found a כֹּפֶר” (Job 33:23–24), and Yahweh gives nations as Israel’s ransom, “in your place” (Isa 43:3–4). Jesus says the Son of Man came to give his life a ransom (λύτρον, the Greek given for כֹּפֶר at Pro 13:8) for many (Mat 20:28; Mrk 10:45), and Paul that he gave himself a ransom for all (1Ti 2:6).

On the tenth day of the seventh month is יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים: Israel holds a holy assembly, humbles their souls and does no work, “for it is a day of כִּפֻּרִים, to make a covering for you before Yahweh your God”, and whoever does not humble himself that day is cut off (Lev 23:27–32). Lev 16 sets out what is done. Only the high priest goes inside the curtain, once a year, with blood, and sprinkles it on the כַּפֹּרֶת and before it (Lev 16:2, 14–15); he purges the holy place, the tent and the altar of Israel’s uncleannesses and makes a covering for the priests and all the people (Lev 16:16–20, 33), and the living goat carries all their iniquities away into the wilderness (Lev 16:21–22). The result is stated: “from all your sins you will be clean before Yahweh” (Lev 16:30). On this day the horn proclaims liberty in the jubilee year (Lev 25:9–10). Hebrews reads the day as pointing beyond itself: the high priest went in once a year, not without blood (Heb 9:7), and the yearly repetition was a reminder of sins, since the blood of bulls and goats cannot take sins away (Heb 10:1–4); Christ entered the holy place once for all by his own blood, obtaining eternal redemption (Heb 9:11–12), and by one offering has perfected for all time those who are made holy (Heb 10:14).

Yahweh says he will meet Moses and speak with him “from above the כַּפֹּרֶת, from between the two cherubim” (Exo 25:22; Num 7:89), and that he appears in the cloud over it (Lev 16:2). On יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים the blood of the sin offerings is sprinkled on it and before it (Lev 16:14–15): the place where Yahweh met his people is the place where blood was put to take their sins away. Hebrews names it with the Greek ἱλαστήριον (Heb 9:5), and Paul says that God set forth Christ Jesus as a ἱλαστήριον through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness in passing over sins done before (Rom 3:25). John calls him the ἱλασμός, the Greek given for כִּפֻּרִים (Lev 25:9), for our sins, and not for ours only but for the whole world’s (1Jn 2:2), sent because God loved us (1Jn 4:10).
